utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. We are to commence this morning with submissions in respect of the question of how to proceed with the motion as to the fitness of the accused to be tried. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I have asked Mr. Weiner to address the Prosecution submissions, and I will turn it over to him if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Not wanting to discourage you, Mr. Weiner, I think I did say yesterday that we saw no need for lengthy submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I will be brief, Your Honour. It is our -- it is the Prosecutor's argument that an evidentiary hearing is not required on three grounds. First, that there is no requirement in the Rules or in the Statute for an evidentiary hearing for this type of procedure. Number two, the comprehensive nature of the medical reports eliminates the need for an evidentiary hearing. And number three, the circumstances of this case indicate that an evidentiary hearing is not required. First, the Rules and Statute do not require a hearing. Rule 74 bis authorises a medical examination of an accused. The Rule, however, has no provision requiring an evidentiary hearing based on the reports of those experts or the examinations of those experts. Article 21(4)(e) of the Statute states: "An accused has the right to examine or have examined the witnesses against him." That's what it states in its pertinent part. Here, the doctors are providing information as to the accused's competency to stand trial or his fitness to stand trial and are not providing information against him. They are not providing information to prove any of the charges. They are not providing any information relating to the indictment. Consequently, that Article does not require an evidentiary hearing. If we look at the Rules, we look at the Statute, there is no requirement for an evidentiary hearing. Rather, it's a matter in the discretion of the Chamber. Two, the reports in this case are sufficient for determining this issue. The Defence has provided a psychiatric report, a supplement to it, medical reports from Montenegro. We also have medical reports from Bronovo hospital and the Detention Unit. The Prosecution has provided reports, a psychiatric report from three eminent psychologists, two neuropsychiatrists, a geriatric psychiatrist, as well as comments from a neuroradiologist. With this extensive report, which includes not only an examination but also discusses the issues which were raised or the tests which were raised in Kovacevic which the Kovacevic court felt was the basis for fitness, having these comprehensive reports, what would a hearing add? What would be achieved from a hearing? We have all the facts before us. We have sufficient facts. And the third statement or the third matter for argument is the circumstances in this case does not mandate a hearing or an evidentiary hearing. This case is different from most matters where competency or fitness to be tried is heard. Usually, it's a pre-trial matter. The Court has had little or no opportunity to observe the accused in most pre-trial matters. That isn't the situation here. We have been on trial since December 16th. That's three-and-a-half months. The Court's had the opportunity to observe the accused, to converse with the accused, and to observe the accused's interaction with counsel. The Court's ability to observe and listen to the accused, combined with the comprehensive psychiatric reports are sufficient to determine the accused's competency or fitness to stand trial. Therefore, it is our position that no evidentiary hearing would be necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It is the position of the Defence with respect to this issue that we hold a different position, in fact, of what my colleague said a moment ago. So I'd like to start off by presenting certain facts linked to the medical report which was submitted by the Prosecution. The Defence has not understood this opportunity as being one occasioning putting forth arguments contained in the report itself. I understood this hearing to be one in which we should decide our future conduct on the issue and in the matter. Now, what springs to mind at first glance when we're talking about the Prosecution medical report, and let me repeat that I'm not going to go into detail. I'd just like to bring certain facets up. There are certain shortcomings in that report which make it completely inappropriate and unsuitable to the situation we find ourselves in. Your Honour, I'm going to mention at this juncture just a few points. The report which you have before you and which I'm sure you have read through is quite simply a report which is based on one single diagnostic method, that is to say, it is founded on a conversation and interview with the accused held in the Detention Unit, and it is based on quotations from the transcript and from the hearings in the courtroom. Modern psychiatry, that is to say, in the last 50 years, has not based a single of its conclusions on things like this, that is to say, what somebody's mental capacities are in any respect, capacities generally and mental capacities, are based solely and exclusively on a conversation held with the individual. I can see that no other diagnostic method was applied. There were no psychiatric tests, and we all know that psychiatric tests have become a basic instrument for establishing about what we wish to know about the mental health and health in general of a patient. And that was not resorted to or applied in this particular case. The Defence report that you had before you was based on a whole battery of tests which were applied, which were used with the patient on the basis of which we drew our conclusions. So, Your Honours, with all due respect to the work undertaken by the medical experts of the Prosecution, they did not contain anything of that kind. And therefore, the report is completely incompatible with what the Defence report has done. And it is inadequate and does not correspond -- it does not, as I say, correspond to the questions that were broached and raised in the Defence report. So with all due respect, it is a superficial, one-sided report which does not give us -- them the possibility of drawing the necessary conclusions, conclusions necessary to this Trial Chamber for it to assume a position with respect to the capabilities of the accused to follow his trial. As an illustration, l should like to mention the fact that, for example, what pursuant to your instructions should be done, a scan -- a head scan of the accused, the position in that regard was established by the fact that somebody called up one of the experts and told them of their view. There is no written trace, no document, no explanation on the basis of which we would be able to weigh up how any of the conclusions were drawn. How can a radiologist state his views with respect to a medical problem over the phone? And the fact that this was communicated over the phone, this can give us as the Defence team grounds to ask questions. How can we speak in an argumented way when we are talking about a telephone conversation and report? And another interesting point is that the report does actually in basic terms confirm the Defence's position, or rather the expert Defence witness with respect to dementia. The consequences to be drawn from all this are, of course, quite different. Since the other two diagnoses that were reached have been rejected in -- that is to say, the diagnosis presented by the Defence with respect to PTSD and depression, and there is no argumentation for that. There are Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. no tests on the basis of which something like that was established and which would warrant a conclusion of that kind. So what is the Defence position and proposal, faced with a situation of this kind? As the report has these shortcomings, and as those shortcomings, as I have tried very briefly, and I emphasise briefly, to address, the Defence sees no other way but to tell the people who compiled the report that it needs to ask them questions in cross-examination to hear their views with respect to all the areas in which the report has its shortcomings. Now, with respect to the arguments put forth by my learned colleague, here, Your Honours, we are not dealing with Rule 74 and its realm of expertise. What we were asked to do was that the parties should tender their medical reports, and the Trial Chamber, Your Honours, when we asked for an expert witness pursuant to Rule 74 to be brought in was not accepted, which means that we're not dealing with something that was clearly set by the Court, by the Trial Chamber. We are not in a situation in which the expert witnesses where nominated and appointed by the Trial Chamber. Quite the contrary. The parties were called upon to present their arguments. So any conclusions drawn from that to the effect that Rule 74 does not call for any examination or further examining of the report stands at this point. Let me just mention, Your Honours, something that I'm sure you happened to notice in reading through this report. The report does not, in a single word, mention the influences of somatic diseases which the accused is suffering from which are exceptionally important for his overall mental health and general health to follow this trial. So this whole complex of questions have not been addressed. It has been left out and set apart from the final conclusion that the psychiatrists reached, those who were engaged by the Prosecution. Similarly, the method in which they selected positions in this report and the opinions from previous medical findings is highly selective, very dubious, and therefore all those are the reasons for which we wish to show the individuals compiling the reports their opinions and to ask for their positions on other portions of all the other reports that have been supplied. And this has been ignored to date. Their approach has been a selective one. Their approach has been one which does not enable you, Your Honours, should you wish to base your positions on their report, arrive at the proper conclusions, one that would be -- conclusions that would be just and fair. Therefore, what we should like to suggest at this point is that you enable us to examine all the medical experts provided by the Prosecution, or one of them. This won't take up too much of the Court's time. But it is something that we consider to be absolutely necessary. From experience gained so far working at this Tribunal, in all similar situations which have to do with the establishment of the psychological capabilities and capacities of the accused, what I can say with absolute certainty is that tests were conducted, psychiatric and psychological tests were performed, so they are exact indicators. They can be measured. And on the basis of such parameters, can an objective conclusion be drawn, which would be rid of all other influences and implications that can come into play in cases of this kind. So all those reports were done on the basis of that. The first that was offered to one of the Trial Chambers was the one that was offered to you, too, in this particular case. I'm not going to go in an open session into the details of which cases such tests were resorted to, although I would be happy and glad to do so, in order to indicate how it was done, even in those examples in which the Prosecution today or in the previous days in addressing the matter applied and brought up. Therefore, this is our request and our proposal to Your Honours: It is that we are given the opportunity of considering the report in this courtroom. We consider it to be unfounded, incorrect, and we desire to present that to you, Your Honours. We have no other way of doing this but to do it in court. So with the Court's indulgence, we ask that an examination of those witnesses be organised so that we can question them. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to respond in two sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That the tests performed by our experts were part of a multidisciplinary evaluation by both American and European experts, eminent American and European experts, one who is a B/C/S speaker, and that the tests were sufficient and the report is, in fact, comprehensive. And as previously stated, that there is no need for any additional hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will give some consideration to these submissions and let you have a decision probably tomorrow. Thank you. Right. Are you ready with the next witness, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: He should be here, Your Honour. I have not been informed that he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the witness could be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for interrupting your instructions as to the next step in these proceedings. But I'm wondering whether perhaps this would be a good moment for us to say a few words about what is contained in our submission with respect to the transcripts of the fifth and sixth interview of Admiral Jokic which we were supplied under the circumstances that I'm sure you're aware of. So may I address that matter now, or do you think another situation would be more opportune?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, we have your submission. But it didn't seem to us to be one that required further oral submission. You have covered this ground quite a bit already in two lots of oral submission. We grasp fully what you're saying, and we are going to discuss it together later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any burning need on the part of the Prosecution to put any submission about that? It seems to us you've already spoken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Chamber knows our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. And thank you for coming. I'm sorry that you were not able to be reached yesterday. Would you be kind enough to take the affirmation card and read the affirmation, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fietelaars. Would you please for the record give us your complete name.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: My name is Johannes Hubertus Wilhemus Fietelaars.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And your date of birth, please, place of birth and nationality.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The 9th of December 1936, and my nationality is Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you presently employed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, madam. I am retired, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: From what you have retired, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: From a diplomatic career in the Dutch foreign ministry. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I take you through with the Chamber's permission with a bit of quickening your diplomatic career. Let us start from 1964. Would you indicate, please, what assignments you had in the Dutch foreign ministry at that time.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: At that time, I was a trainee in the Dutch foreign ministry, and I was appointed to my first posting in Wellington, New Zealand, as third secretary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For what type of affairs?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I did legal affairs, I did consular affairs, and I did trade matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving along to 1966, where was your next posting, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Liberia, Monrovia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As what?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution and witness make a pause between their questions and answers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My apologies to the translation section.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question, Mr. Fietelaars, for the benefit of the translators. Your second posting in 1966?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Monrovia in Liberia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In what capacity, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: As number two and general dog's body [sic], because it was only a two-diplomat post.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: 1967, your posting?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: 1967, I went to London in Great Britain.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And in what capacity, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Number two in the commercial section of the embassy.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: 1969, I transferred to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, as number two of the embassy. In general charge of everything that was not a direct responsibility of the ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Then 1969 to 1970.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I transferred from Kuala Lumpur to Singapore because of the political changes in that region. And I finished my four-year stint there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you also --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Number two in the embassy, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I went to Brussels with the Dutch representation with the European communities, and I became first secretary and later in the assignment counsellor for nuclear and environmental affairs.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: 1978, I was transferred to the Royal Netherlands embassy in Lima, Peru, as the number two and the officer in charge of the Dutch development aid programme.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: In 1981 I was transferred in preparation of royal visit and the Olympic games to Los Angeles as consul general.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: 1985 I was, after a career abroad, for the first time recalled to the ministry in The Hague, and I became inspector of the diplomatic service.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was your rank while you held that position?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Ambassador, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: 1988, I changed within the ministry to the chair of director for European integration. My team started writing the Maastricht Treaty.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: 1990, I was appointed Ambassador to Belgrade, Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did you have any dealings with any other parts of the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, I was at the same time appointed Ambassador to Albania. Nonresident, but operating out of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: 1992, what occurred with EU Ambassadors?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: In 1992, the consul of ministers in Brussels decided that all Ambassadors of the EU countries were going to be recalled for consultations, which is in fact a cryptic remark for recall because of the unhappiness with regard to the political developments in the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where did you come back to when you left Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: When I left Yugoslavia, I attended a number of assignments that the then foreign minister Hans Van den Broek gave me in connection with the Balkans for about -- a bit more than -- a bit less than a year. And then I was transferred to my next post.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you retain while you were outside of Yugoslavia the ambassador title?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Ambassadorial rank, yes. And also because my function in Albania was uninterrupted and unaffected by the developments in the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And where were you physically operating from?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: From The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: 1993, I was appointed Ambassador to Ottawa, Canada.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Ambassador to Copenhagen, Denmark.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel and the witness please slow down for interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let me go back. 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: 1993, I was appointed Ambassador to Ottawa, Canada.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: 1998, I was transferred to Copenhagen in Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you retire after that posting?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. I retired in January 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your formal post-high school education. What are you trained in formally and where did you train?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I have a masters degree in civil and penal law at the Dutch University of Leiden.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As ambassador to Yugoslavia, did you find yourself having frequent contact, particularly in 1991, with the ministry of Defence in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. In 1991, Luxembourg, one of the member states of the European Union, had the Presidency of the European Union without having a resident ambassador in Belgrade. Now, there is a custom and a treaty between the Netherlands and Luxembourg that look after their interests in such situations, which meant that a Dutch ambassador became the formal representative of the presidency of the European Union, reporting to both Luxembourg and to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you had contact with the ministry of Defence in Belgrade, with whom did you directly have contact?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, on the whole, it was at the level of -- not the Supreme Command, which was the presidency of the Federal Republic, but with the actual command of the JNA which at that time I think was General Kadijevic and his number two, Admiral Brovet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have regular or relatively regular contact with both of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. As the situation developed, the concern in the capitals in Europe, and therefore the concern in Brussels increased, and I received regular and in the course of time more frequent instructions to go and discuss the military situation with the top of the ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have face-to-face meetings with both General Kadijevic and Admiral Brovet?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you become aware of a conflict arising in the territory of the area of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. This was very much public. You saw daily on television in Belgrade and also all kinds of references in my direct Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. business instructions refer to the developments in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you have a military attache component to the embassy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. We had a four-person office. The military attache, the deputy military attache, a researcher, and an archivist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you come to learn of shellings by the JNA on Dubrovnik at the end of October 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did you come to learn about these incidents?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: We had regular contact with two Dutch journalists who operated in the region between southern Montenegro and the Albanian border and who were at that time resident in Dubrovnik. And also, the then mayor of Dubrovnik regularly phoned the Netherlands embassy informing us, me and my collaborators, of the developments within his city.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Netherlands was holding the presidency of the EU at the time? I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The Netherlands embassy handled the presidency in Belgrade on behalf of Luxembourg until the 1st of July. After the 1st of July, I did that on behalf of the Netherlands. So the time that we are talking about now, early 1991, I did it on behalf of the Luxembourg presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was your reaction to the information you had received about the shellings in Dubrovnik? Let us say the 23rd of October, 23rd, 24th of October. What, if any, action did you take?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Immediately informed The Hague and Luxembourg about this and requested instructions in order to see whether or not I should verify in Belgrade with the Yugoslav authorities what was reported to us as going on by the Croatians in and around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I sent them a telegram, a long telegram, and told them about what we were receiving as information out of the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you instructed to make contact with any members of the --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Almost -- I think the day after I sent my report, I got instructions to go and see the top of the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did you make an appointment and see someone at the top of the defence ministry? If so, whom?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I did. And although I should refer to my notes before I say it with absolute certainty, but I think I had an appointment with Admiral Brovet then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What do you -- what, if you recall, and certainly we will circulate as exhibits some of your notes, but what is your recollection of your conversation with Admiral Brovet about the events in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, the long and short of it was that he denied ever taking any initiative in shelling or damaging Dubrovnik, and that the only thing they did was react to provocations by the Croatian irregulars. And they did not recognise that Croatia at the time had an army, so they talked about Croatian irregulars.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me just a minute, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I take you back to a day -- well, do you remember the date you called Admiral Brovet?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recall meetings on the 22nd of October with -- do you recall a series of three meetings you had in connection with the --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, about those three meetings.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: That is still rather clear in my mind because it was a very busy day. My number two visited the JNA, the defence ministry in order to meet Mr. Brovet. I think he was accompanied by one or two others of whom the names are in my notes that I put at your disposal. In the early afternoon, the head of the monitor mission of the European Union, Ambassador van Houten, saw him, and late in the afternoon I went over there for a general discussion on the things that had been discussed in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I may ask the usher to please distribute documents -- they are a packet of documents that was provided from Mr. Fietelaars, and the particular letters we will be looking at are G and F. As well as H. H, G, F, please. Mr. Fietelaars, these three documents, I believe, may assist in helping us run through the meetings. First of all, can you tell us about the documents that you have in front of you. Are these documents that are compiled by the embassy, by yourself, or by someone under your direction?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Ma'am, before I answer may I ask you, am I supposed to have three documents in front of me? I have G and H.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You should have G, H, and F.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I have no F here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And they will also be put up on the Sanction as we go through them, which is the computerised evidence. I will repeat my question, sir. The documents that you have in front of you, were these documents that were compiled by the embassy in connection with its work, and particularly in connection with meetings that may have taken place in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Let me say first that we had an extremely busy time in the embassy. There was a lot of work, and we were not overstaffed. So we developed the habit that once such a thing was done, the first thing was to go back to the embassy, get your recollection down on paper, get them typed out and everything, and then correct them for style and for additional remarks. And then send them, the first possible of radio contact to The Hague and to Luxembourg. At the times we're talking about now, I'm talking about only The Hague because the Luxembourg presidency was over. I did the same thing. These documents I wrote after my meeting with Admiral Brovet. I corrected them first thing in the morning, of the morning after when they had been typed out, and then they were sent in the course of the morning to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You had taken notes then from which you compiled --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, and recollections. Because what is on paper here is more than the shorthand notes that I -- not shorthand, but very, very abbreviated notes that I took during the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. And looking at these three documents that we have for convenience marked as F, G, and H, can you please give us from them indications of what meetings you had with Admiral Brovet or any other high-ranking persons in the ministry of Defence in Belgrade concerning the situation in Dubrovnik at that time.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The first meeting was a meeting that took place in the morning, attended by my number two in the ministry -- in the embassy, Mr. Dirk Hasselman. And Ambassador van Houten was present, and Ambassador Perrin.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now which particular document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I am referring to the first line in document F.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And can you indicate what was the subject of discussion? What did you bring to the attention of Admiral Brovet?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, we discussed more things than Dubrovnik. But about Dubrovnik, I told Admiral Brovet that we had new information about increased shelling of Dubrovnik and considerable damage in the suburbs around Dubrovnik. And the stories about how threatened the civilian population felt in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I turn your attention to the English translation on page 2 of document F.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where it is said: "With regard to Dubrovnik, Brovet made clear once again that the JNA troops have orders to spare the Old Town." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did the topic of the Old Town come up?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Because I reported that the telephone informations that I got specifically to severe damage of the suburbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We're talking about the 22nd of -- of the suburbs, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you very much. Were you given earlier assurances about protections of the Old Town, or was this the first time it had come up?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, ma'am. This kind of thing came up regularly, whenever you discussed conflict, it came up in discussions around Vukovar, about Osijek, and other things. The first remark our discussion partners usually made was that the JNA was not run by a number of uncultured people and barbarians, but people who were very much aware how much culture there was in the different parts of the Republic of Yugoslavia. And that they were committed to protecting them and to -- to protect them as much as possible. But of course, when they were provoked, then a retaliation and self-protection had to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In Document G, this is another -- does this also cover some of the aspects of the meetings that were held the day before you contacted Admiral Brovet about the shellings? We're talking about the 22nd now.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Could you rephrase -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is on the 22nd. Now, was there a second discussion or any further discussion that the provisions of which are found in Document G about the situation in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yeah. On the 22nd of October, the Ambassador van Houten and Mr. Brovet had a discussion together. And there, again, Mr. Brovet stated that the actual leadership of the army was not always responsible for the things that were decided, but that they were bound by instruction of the supreme commander, which at that moment in time was Mr. Kostic, the president of the presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention, if I may, to the first page of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where there is a discussion about the chief of command acting out of concern for the threat on Montenegro caused by the Croats, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was the position that the European delegations or the Europeans were trying to protect relative to Dubrovnik? Was there a concern in particular --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- that was being addressed?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: In my telephone conversations that I had with The Hague, the point of the Dubrovnik status in the context of world cultural Heritage came up, and both within myself, but also within the mind of my contact at The Hague side, it was obvious that this was a point that was going to play very heavily in the discussions that European member states would hold about the evaluation of the developments in and around Dubrovnik. So I very specifically mentioned that this cultural heritage aspect and the status that Dubrovnik had in the context of decisions of UNESCO as very important and that it was totally unsupportable and unsufferable that again such a status that had been agreed by all member states of UNESCO, that that would be denied for tactical propositions and that that was unthinkable. And in that context, they said that they had their major strategic concerns as well, except for tactical things, and they were protecting their -- the member states of the Federal Republic, and especially the threat that was now becoming clearly visible towards Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In your discussions, was there a connection between this particular set of comments and the representation by Admiral Brovet that the JNA units had been instructed not to touch Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Would you repeat that, please, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes. In connection with the discussions you have just mentioned, was there a nexus to Admiral Brovet's having indicated that the JNA had been ordered -- the troops of the JNA had been ordered not to touch the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, the gist of what the commanders, because I don't specifically remember if it was only Brovet or on another occasion also General Kadijevic, it was that -- I should not be all that preoccupied because the whole thing was already over as far as the JNA was concerned, that what they wanted to achieve had been achieved. And that if any further contrary happenings would take place there, it would be fault of the Croats rather than the fault of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If -- I'd just ask you to turn your attention to H that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The introductory paragraph contains a comment that the -- I'm sorry. "Along the lines of your 157 it was pointed out in advance that there was no excuse to be found in a necessary defence of a Serbian minority or that justification could be found for Croatian provocations, lack of communication lines or uncontrolled acts of Serbian forces."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was that communicated fully and forcefully to --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, ma'am, because by that time we had decided that things had to be said clearly rather than diplomatically, because it was very difficult to solicit an answer from the other side unless you indicated precisely what you wanted and until you indicated the considerations that moved you to pose such questions, that it was not insolence or anything but real concern. And the feeling that things were happening here that should not be happening in 20th century Europe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask at this time to move these three documents into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document numbers are as follows: Document F is marked P138; Document G, P139; and Document H is P140. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Returning to your having been notified of shelling in the city of Dubrovnik -- against Dubrovnik, on the 23rd of October, did you have a meeting with anyone in the federal ministry? I'm sorry, yeah, the Federal Ministry of Defence. If it would assist, Mr. Fietelaars, I would be happy to present your A, Document A. It would probably be easier to go through it this way, rather than rely strictly on... Do you recognise this particular document, Mr. Fietelaars?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was this a document that was compiled by the -- by yourself or by someone under your direction in connection with your duties in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: This document I've written myself on the night of the day that we visited Dubrovnik and after we had come back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, the date of the visit is 29 October. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In order to arrange this visit, was this visit raised at your discussions with Admiral Brovet on the date of...

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I think I inquired about status of this request that had been originally talked about in a visit by the Italian Ambassador Sergio Vento to Admiral Brovet, and that he said he would inquire. And I asked him when I saw him, I think it was on the 22nd. The status of that -- no. Yes, it must have been the 22nd because it was the last time I saw him before, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you made aware of the shellings against Dubrovnik on the 23rd of October?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And after having been made aware, did you see Admiral Brovet?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I did. And at that meeting it came up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what did you request be done? What did you want to achieve by that meeting and by discussing the --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Cessation of hostilities and protection of the civil population. That was the object of the exercise all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you seek to have a visit to Dubrovnik to see for yourself what had taken place?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, I didn't take the real initiative. The real initiative was taken a couple of days earlier by the Italian Ambassador. And he got a reply from the JNA authorities at the lower level that they would inquire whether or not such a thing would be possible. He told us, and so I inquired the status of that request. And then on the 22nd, Admiral Brovet said to me that they were processing that. And in principle, they would take us there. And they didn't mention a date at the time, but we were informed shortly before the 29th that the visit would take place and that those ambassadors who had beforehand had been vocally critical of the JNA, that they could come along and see for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And which ambassadors would have been included in that delegation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, I think at least the ambassador of Italy was there, because he was the original initiator of the request. The Greek Ambassador was there at his own request, even though he had not been all that critical of the situation. And the United Kingdom was there, the Netherlands was there. And Ambassador Warren Zimmerman of the United States asked if his number two could take part in the trip in order to observe what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was -- were you concerned about the allegations of damage to the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. Because also the telephone calls out of Dubrovnik at that time came in, and to our great surprise, telecommunications were still functioning between Dubrovnik and Belgrade, so every concerned citizen could ring everybody in Belgrade. So our telephone by that time was -- I didn't register all the telephone calls, but the general gist was they are shelling the Old Town, and we got wounded in town, and there's a lot of damage. But that did not refer specifically to the Old Town. That referred to Dubrovnik as the general living place of a number of Croatians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So a visit was arranged through the JNA Ministry of Defence --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- the Federal Ministry of Defence. And do you know at the local level who agreed to the visit and who would -- well, who agreed to the visit?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Admiral Brovet told me that he agreed to the visit, only the date had not been fixed at the time when he told me that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And at the local level in Dubrovnik, were you given any information about who was going to --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, we had in Belgrade Colonel Stojic who was the head of the liaison section between the JNA and the Corps of Defence attaches. He informed us and he briefed us beforehand about what was going to happen. And one of the things that was going to happen was that we would meet in the morning -- that we would meet two highly ranking -- high-ranking JNA officers; one, Admiral Jokic, and the other one General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had you ever had any contact with or any familiarity with Admiral Jokic? Well, other than his name was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, he was pointed out to me at one of my visits as sitting behind General Kadijevic in a meeting where a number of ambassadors visited the JNA. And of course, Admiral Jokic, especially in that period, was rather visible on television in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had you ever seen or had any physical contact with General Strugar at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, ma'am, at least not that I recall or correct. I don't even recall ever --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, how was the trip --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer. It's too fast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Who was the actual trip arranged? What was the logistics to be?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: We were picked up at Belgrade airport, the military part of it, by a passenger plane with JNA markings, and we were brought to the air base of Tivat in southern Croatia. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, where is Tivat, in which republic?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I thought it was still Croatia. Or is it... must be. I don't know, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Feel free to consult your notes certainly. It's not a problem. I believe you have discussed the arrival in your notes. You're more than welcome to take a look at them.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask you, please, tell us, was it an overnight visit or what was it a -- what was the duration?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, ma'am. It was planned as a one-day visit. And you're right, when I look at my notes here, it says it's in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you arrive -- was it planned for morning to evening? What was the general plan of the visit?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The general plan of the visit was to fly out as early as possible and meet with the authorities at Tivat air base. And then take a launch to Dubrovnik because land travel was too dangerous in view of the fact that there was frequent sniper activity along that road, according to the JNA authorities. The road itself was controlled by the JNA, but they judged that it was too dangerous for us. And then they said after you arrive, you will have until about 2.30, because you have to be back in Tivat before 5.00 because you have to fly out during daylight. So we will have an evaluative meeting at the end, and then you will fly back to Belgrade, which would then have been around 5.00. That's what the Colonel Stojic told us in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Is the basic day as it happened captured or summarised in this particular document which is --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- A. Okay. What time did you actually arrive in Tivat?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, we came there at 8.45. Quarter to 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And were you met by any officials of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, we were met by -- we were met by Admiral Jokic and a number of colonels around him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And did Admiral Jokic carry on with the plan as you had understood it to be arranged in Belgrade? What happened upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, he gave us a briefing, which did not bring very much new. It was the official point of view of the JNA. And it was also the point of view expressed by Admiral Jokic, that all this activity of the JNA was based upon extreme provocation by the Croats, and that they had been trying to negotiate for months already to come to a peaceful arrangement which would allow them to retire their equipment and cease their activities. And to no avail.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How long did the briefing last, if you remember, or if it's noted?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I don't know if it's noted, but it must have been somewhere between half an hour and three quarters of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did you actually travel to Dubrovnik? What type of boat was it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No. It was a passenger launch of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Dubrovnik, and at what part or what port did you arrive?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: We arrived at the Venetian port is the southern end, and we took about two-and-a-half hours to get there because the launch was rather slow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, did Admiral Jokic accompany you --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, ma'am, he remained in Tivat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did other persons from the JNA accompany you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, a number of officers. But they never disembarked with us. They stayed onboard with the launch, and as soon as we had disembarked, the launch pulled back and waited in open sea.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were there -- upon your arrival, were there Croatian members of any delegation there to meet you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. The mayor of Dubrovnik was there. And there was also a representative of the Croatian government. I have his name in my notes, if I may refer to that. Excuse me. Well, I do not want to hold up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's okay. We can come back to that. But there was someone, another official --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: There was another official who had come out specifically from Zagreb to accompany us, also, and Mr. Bondioli who was the Dubrovnik head of the monitor mission of the EC. He also was there at the quay to greet us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I see there's the name of Hrvoje Kacic mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the man who met us. We had met him before, because whenever an ambassador travelled to Zagreb he was, together with the chief of protocol, was the first man that he would meet in his visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, when you were having briefings, when you were with the members of the JNA in Tivat, was all communication through interpreters, interpreter/translators?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. The Yugoslavia side only spoke Serbo-Croatian as the language was known then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And were there translator/interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you got to Dubrovnik, did you also --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kacic translated for the mayor, and Mr. Bondioli could communicate with us in French and in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What happened upon arrival at the Venetian port in Dubrovnik. What did you do, by what means did you do it, did you ride, tell us exactly --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: We walked the full-length of the main street of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you say Dubrovnik, are you talking about the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, the Old Town, within the walls.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And this was the 29th of October.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, the 29th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What were your observations about damage, if any, that you may have seen?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: There were three points of damage in the Old Town that were pointed out to us and that we saw ourselves. There was a small hole in the bell tower, which is at one end of the main street. And some streaks of black which indicated that it was caused by an explosion or something like that. And there were two buildings along the street that were identified by the people who accompanied us as a pharmacy and a library. And they had apparently received a grenade or some device through the roof which had blown off the tiles and exposed the beams of the roof construction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As of that date, your overall observation about extent of damage in the Old Town, just as of that time, what was your general observation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, it was not very impressive, although one of the remarks that we heard was that it was a good indication how precisely the JNA could fire if they wanted, that they would hit three buildings which were main parts of the Heritage idea of Dubrovnik. But there was nothing there I personally thought that could not be repaired in a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you remember what time you finished the tour of Dubrovnik? Or did you progress beyond the Old Town? Did you see --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, we went beyond the Old Town. We walked also along -- outside the street, outside of the ramparts that goes parallel to the ramparts and the land side. We saw a couple of hotels that had been totally destroyed. There were two refugee centres where all the glass had been blown out, a lot of glass blown out in the streets, and grenade damage also on the surface of the roads.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How long all in all did you stay in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: We managed to stretch out the visit until about half past 3.00 in the afternoon, while Admiral Jokic had stressed that he needed us back on the launches an hour earlier because of the sniper activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So when you say an hour earlier, it must have been maybe half past 2.00, but you stayed a bit longer?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, we stayed until half past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you returned to what -- where did you return to? The same place you had come?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The same place we came from, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That would be Tivat. How did you get back there?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, the same launch that brought us there picked us up, but then we were told that because we were so late it could not be done leisurely with the launch but that we and needed a faster means of transport. And I think it was a motor torpedo boat that came alongside in mid-sea, and we were invited to -- while they were proceeding, we were invited to step over from one boat to the other. It was a bit of an undignified thing, because it had been a long time since I had done such gymnastic exercises, and some of the gentlemen were a bit older than I was, and it was really a real experience, I can tell you, not to use another word.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. When you returned to Tivat --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: That trip, by the way, from then on lasted less than an hour, while the trip there was two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you got back to Tivat, was it still daylight when you returned to Tivat?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you hold an evaluation meeting to discuss with the persons, with the JNA officials your observations from your trip to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yeah. We were brought into a meeting hall where television cameras were and a number of journalists, Yugoslav journalists, and we were met by two apparently high-ranking officers there who we talked to also by interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was -- again, this was a JNA interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you speak to Admiral Jokic at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, I told him and the other gentleman was standing next to him, so he must have followed it, too, in the translation of the interpreter or direct if he understood anything -- any English, I told him that we were quite upset about the visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated two high-ranking officers. That would have been Admiral Jokic and another person. Were you introduced by title to the other individual that was there?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: In my profession, you either call somebody Mr. with his name after it, or by his title. You don't say Ambassador Fietelaars; you say Mr. Fietelaars or Ambassador. So I said my name because I don't refer to myself as Ambassador. But I don't know because we were listening to the interpreters what the other two said exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you ever -- was a name of the other individual ever provided to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, I thought it was provided to me in the morning by Colonel Stojic who said that we were going to meet two officers, and one would be Admiral Jokic and the other one would be General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But at that time, were you ever actually given the name?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you assume that the individual --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: -- was General Strugar. Okay. What did you tell these two persons you were talking to? What did you communicate about your visit that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, the gist of it was that even though the damage to the Old Town was minor, the general view of Dubrovnik meant that the population of Dubrovnik and the housing and the roads and everything were in severe danger. There was severe damage. And that it was incomprehensible that a civilian population could be so attacked and so threatened while we never observed any military presence in that city.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the atmosphere at this particular meeting, the review. Was it a formal briefing atmosphere or was it a social?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, no, it looked very much like social. We remained standing in little circles, and the people with cameras and microphones came up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were there refreshments served?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, we got drinks and...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you -- were you satisfied with the amount of time you had gotten in the -- in Dubrovnik? Did you think your visit was sufficiently long for you to gather as much information as you wanted to gather?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, certainly not. Because a lot of people in the population had hoped to talk with us, and we just had to say, "No, we have to walk on because we want to see as much as possible, and please talk to your own representatives, and they will transmit to us any preoccupation that you have and we will try to act on it as much as possible." But yes, I would have liked to remain there for a couple of hours more. And that is also what caused the delay. We talked to people, and especially with people who only spoke Serbo-Croatian, that slows down conversation quite a lot, the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm terribly sorry. In your Document A, on the page which bears the identifying number of 03521743, it would be -- the last numbers are 1743, you have made a note that: "Now JNA forces surround Dubrovnik looking down on it from positions..." - toward the bottom - "in the surrounding hills at Dubac, at Ivanica (on the Bosnian border) and at the opposite side of the Dubrovnik river. The Admiral...", is this Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: "The Admiral said, that the JNA has no further objectives in the Dubrovnik area. There was no threat any more to the JNA. The only thing that had still to be done was to clear the region of all weapons and to make certain that the tens of dead and hundreds of wounded had not been sacrificed without cause. In the discussion that followed, the Admiral admitted that the Croatians could not do any harm to the JNA forces in the region, and that there had only been minor provocations since the cease-fire since 29 October 1991 at 1700 hours."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yeah, by then everything was silent, they said. So there was no provocation, and there was no activity from the JNA side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there any further discussion about the continued presence of the JNA if all objectives had been reached between you and the Admiral?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: We underlined that if all objectives had been reached there was no reason to give all that heavy ordinance in the hills directed towards Dubrovnik, and what did they plan to do? The Admiral said, you know, we have been here are our ordinance, and no gun was ever turned on the old city of Dubrovnik, and not a single stone of Dubrovnik was touched except when we retaliated rather than attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did you tell the Admiral about your observations of the damage in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And I note on the page after which we were just reading, that would be the one ending in 1744, I believe you just said -- now, is this the Admiral speaking, that no gun was ever turned on the old city of Dubrovnik, no single stone in Dubrovnik was touched?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes. Except --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was this in the face of your having indicated that there was damage --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: There was severe destruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Severe destruction. I'm talking about the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: In the Old Town, I told him about the three hits that we saw and observed ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It goes on to say that: "There is no destruction of Dubrovnik, there will be none depending on how fast we can find a final solution." What was your understanding, if any, about the continued presence of the JNA heavy weaponry you just referred to? Was it -- was there an indication that it would remain in the area?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: There was no indication whatsoever. They didn't react to it. So the next time I brought it up in Belgrade with Admiral Brovet. And he said as soon as we find a general solution, all these movements will be made and peace will be restored as soon as we have confiscated all the illegal weaponry that's in the region. But that was the only answer we ever got to the displacement possibilities of the ordinance that the JNA had at its disposal in the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I turn your attention to the page ending in 1745, that would be the next page, where it appears -- is this your summary of observations about the damage to the old city, the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The first full linear --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: In the old city, yes, ma'am, that's the...

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the comment -- there's a comment made below that starts: "The randomness of the damage seems to prove the point."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What led you to make that comment about the randomness of the damage?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: There was no obviously directed fire to the suburbs. It was just general destructions. There was not a single building of which one could indicate it had strategic value, that it was a lookout post for military activity or for snipers or for mortar locations. Nothing. There were hotels --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I'm really referring -- does this refer to the Old Town, this comment about randomness? If it does not, then --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: It does not really.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask to move this document into evidence. And is this a convenient time after that, Your Honours, for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before that occurs, while you were Document A in front of you, Mr. Fietelaars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The second page, 1743 in English, very near the bottom at the end of the last full paragraph, you speak of a cease-fire of the 29th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your visit was on the 28th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our visit was on the 29th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And so -- but this is a cease-fire at 5.00 in the afternoon of the 29th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was negotiated directly between the JNA, the head of mission for the monitor mission, and representatives that flew out of The Hague, I think, and it was done in Belgrade and in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So the comment of Admiral Jokic that there had been only minor provocations, he could only have been speaking of one or two hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were there, sir, it was silent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document titled A will be P141.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will now have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Fietelaars, I have been asked by the translation personnel, colleagues, to please for both of us to speak slowly enough so that they can catch question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Following your -- well, let's actually go back. What time did you leave Tivat for Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: It must have been after 9.00 because we arrived in Belgrade at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And on the 1st of November, did you have a meeting with Admiral Brovet concerning your visit and other observations from the visit?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask you, please, to look at Document D, which will be circulated and also is available on Sanction. This document dated 1st of November bearing your name, are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And was this document made in the course of your duties in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. This was a report of the embassy to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The subject of the document is a visit to Admiral Brovet on 1 November. What was the purpose of the visit? What was discussed? And what did you come away from that meeting with?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting happened because the British ambassador phoned me early in the morning saying that he was under instruction to go to the ministry of Defence and express Her Majesty's preoccupation with what was going on in and around Dubrovnik. He phoned me then asking if that would be feasible in the context of the fact that I was writing the general report which would also reach London, being one of the capitals of the EU countries. And how to go about it. I then suggested to him that we will go with a number of EU ambassadors without actually defining the juridical status of this group, and operate as a group of European nations also accompanied by the US embassy because they were present at the visit on the 29th in Dubrovnik. This is what we did. So the British ambassador in the course of that meeting got the possibility to execute his instructions and to express her British Majesty government's preoccupation with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On the first page of this document, the bottom, there is a reference to the next issue to be discussed was how disconcerted the western's world public opinion is with regards to the humanitarian situation in Dubrovnik. Ambassador Hall pointed out that despite the material damage to the old city being small, we regarded the situation of the inhabitants as very precarious. Can you elaborate a bit more. When you say inhabitants, are you talking about the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Civilian population of Dubrovnik, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what in particular underlay this concern for the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, our concern was that we had observed and that we had been told that the city was being starved of supplies and of drinking water and everything, and that survival within the city became more difficult by the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What was -- or how was this addressed by Admiral Brovet?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, once again, we got the standard replies, that the function of the JNA as one of the pillars of state was to re-establish calm and peace in all the regions of the country. And they had to prevent that the Serbian minorities in that area would be massacred. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sorry. Was this part of a reply by Admiral Brovet commenting about the Serbian minorities?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The other part was that also a lot of very precious and costly equipment of the JNA was still within the reach of the irregulars in Dubrovnik, and that had to be salvaged by the JNA as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This again was Admiral Brovet's --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: A remark by Admiral Brovet, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At the top of the second page, Ambassador Hall, I believe is the person referred to by "he."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Stressed the positions taken by the community, that the siege of Dubrovnik should be lifted immediately and that the supplies and the public services to the city have to be mended. What was the response by Admiral Brovet to addressing these concerns?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Admiral Brovet said that he would love to do that, but it was impossible because you cannot solve a little part of a big puzzle by addressing only the little part. Everything was linked to everything, and a general cease-fire, which would be justified by the European authorities, had to be found in the cooperation of the member states of the EU in The Hague, together with Yugoslavia, of course. And that that -- in the context of that occurrence, the total withdrawal of the JNA from that region could be considered. And until such time that there was a solution, it could not because of the dangers for the large Serbian minority that lived in the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I note in the first full -- second full but fuller than the first paragraph, there was nothing that the army would like to do more. This is Admiral Brovet speaking, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, Admiral Brovet speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There is nothing that the army --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: "That the army would like to do more than to retreat."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: "But until a definitive political solution in The Hague by the European community would be found, withdrawing from the crisis areas in Croatia was out of the question, because otherwise the so much dreaded mass murder would start immediately."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you -- a little bit below, did you respond to your views about the civilian population as a -- I think the term used is reprisal? If you look below in the paragraph starting with Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For the benefit of the interpreters: "I have told him, being emphatically seconded on this, and in strong wording by the American second in this, that the holding hostage of a civilian population as a reprisal for the mistreatment of JNA militaries was plainly unacceptable. Dubrovnik did not have a military function." The Admiral replied to this how? Admiral Brovet.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, he denied that that was the case. He said that there was a danger emanating from there, that there were tens of deads and hundreds of wounded in the JNA, and that the situation had to be brought under control because Dubrovnik was a military target. It was a militarily reinforced city. That was the little term that he used.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I could ask you, please, if you could slowly let us know what the Admiral's assertion was, where it says, "The Admiral denied this."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
