utterances.text: If you could read from there.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: And the following sentence is a direct quote from what he said: "Dubrovnik is a militarily reinforced city with cannons and mortars and with thousands of Croatian troops. While the authorities refused to negotiate with the local JNA leadership about the reparation of the normal functioning of the city."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you were in Dubrovnik, did you see thousands of Croatian troops?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The discussions that you had with Admiral Jokic at your meeting on the 29th of October, are these also encapsulated in this particular summary where you say, on the same page: "Admiral Jokic has assured us on 29 October last that all military objectives in the south Dalmatian region have been attained, and that Dubrovnik did not pose a single threat any more for the JNA. Why does the JNA insist on continuing military operations in spite of that?" The response of Admiral Brovet to that was how, in the next sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes. Admiral Brovet could ultimately, because he hummed and hawed a little bit, searching for words, he could only reply that JNA officers and soldiers were threatened, captured, injured and killed everywhere in Croatia, and that all was connected to one another. In that context, we told him that to use a civilian population, hold them hostage, shell them, destroy their houses, take away their supplies, is not a way in which you respond to a military threat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask that this document be moved into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D will be labelled as P142.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Moving on in time, did you become aware of a shelling -- of shelling on Dubrovnik on the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes. There again, contacts out of Dubrovnik, but I think also general news missions in Belgrade referred to new unrest in the region in and around Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask, please, that Document C be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Mr. Fietelaars, which bears the date of 6 December 1991 with the name Hasselman. And if you could remind us who Hasselman is, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasselman was the second-in-command consular of embassy in the Netherlands embassy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was this document compiled at your request or at the request of someone directly under you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yeah. It was prepared for my signature by -- for my authorisation by the time I would come back to the embassy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is called a demarche to General Kadijevic. Can you explain what demarche is?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: A demarche is an intervention with an opposite discussion partner upon instructions received from the foreign ministry where you are instructed to go and tell them of the concerns as enumerated by the foreign ministry, and then leave a written note behind as a summary of the things that you have said, a formal summary of the things that you have said.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In the first part of this document called a demarche, there is a reference made to the meeting with Admiral Brovet on 6 December 1991. And the purpose of the demarche was to urge the JNA to comply with the cease-fire agreement of November 23rd and with Security Council Resolution 71 of November 27th. Can you just give us briefly a little background to the cease-fire negotiations that are discussed. And were they part of a greater plan that would also have encompassed or had impact upon the Dubrovnik region?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: There was a -- I don't know exactly how to start to address your question. Would you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let's take it in parts.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Let's take it in parts. Was there going on in other parts of Europe a series of negotiations to try to bring the hostilities to an end?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. In The Hague, Mr. Lambuca [phoen] developed a plan to try under the aegis of the European Union to broker an agreement between the different parties without addressing any of the big political questions, but just to make certain that the intensity of military activities would be lowered to a full cease-fire. And that was -- was kind of coordinated out of The Hague through meetings that took place both in Brussels and in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There is also mention in this document about a Geneva agreement. It appears on page 03521752. That's the number in the upper right-hand corner. Can you comment about that, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: When other countries became involved and wanted to become involved, for instance, the Soviet Union and the United States, it was logical to make this into an activity that would be carried out in the context of the United Nations. And for that, Geneva was the logical place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: At this particular meeting, at the top of the same page, there is an indication that it was asked to comment on reports received in the course of the day concerning new shelling of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It says: "Kadijevic did not try to bring forward any justification, but promised that an investigation would immediately be ordered."

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was there a -- any understanding about further reporting on results of any such investigation?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. In the first place, I think that the gist of the intervention of General Kadijevic was that he was not aware of the fact that these developments were taking place and that that was why he could not comment on it, and that is why he would have order a -- would order a direct investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Was that your perception?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just your perception.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: But the promise that we will be informed as quickly as possible was not a perception because it was part of the intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask, please, to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document C is labelled P143.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May we please, before you sit down, Mr. Usher, ask for the document bearing "B" to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Fietelaars, do you recognise this document, which is dated 13 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And what is it, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: It is a report of Mr. Hasselman sent out under his name. He was charge d'affair at the moment because I was absent from the post.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And you ordered this to be done, or you --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: -- this was when I -- when I left the post -- left out -- for outside Yugoslavia, I gave him full powers to do exactly as I would do in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. This is a summary of a meeting, is that correct, between -- between and among what persons?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: EU -- EC representatives, we were still then I think, and the Soviet Ambassador and the -- the Russian Ambassador and representative of the United States, Warren Zimmerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And it was with whom in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: It was with Admiral Brovet, as far as I recall. But it's mentioned in the report, I think. And the -- and the same interventions were going to be made in -- in Belgrade and in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In this particular document, on the second page, there is a mention -- the second page is ending in 1748, it -- there is a reference to -- actually, it's the first full paragraph, "those who are" -- let me back up, please. "As far as irregular armed forces are concerned, the Admiral stated that the JNA has taken rigorous measures to bring all units under strict control in the areas where the JNA is responsible. Commanders who fail to implement these measures will be removed. Those who are responsible for the recent shelling of Dubrovnik's old city are now under criminal investigation and have been relieved of their command. The Admiral expressed his regret for the damage inflicted. The JNA has always and will always respect the cultural heritage." Are you aware of what discussions may have taken place about the damage to the Old Town that brought about this series of reactions from Admiral Brovet? Did Mr. Hasselman inform you, or --

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I think that this is an intervention by Admiral Brovet and is based upon his internal instructions within the JNA to have an investigation. I am not aware that before he came to his conclusions he consulted any other source of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Were you or any of the ambassadors with whom you had contact ever informed specifically of the actual results of any investigation into the shelling of Dubrovnik and criminal responsibility therefore by commanders?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Up until the time you retired -- let's back up. Up until the time you left Yugoslavia, had you ever been presented with specific information about investigations, the persons investigated, the persons removed, or was there any follow-up to this representation that is contained in Document B?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would move -- ask to move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document B is labelled P144.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may just take a moment, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Fietelaars, did you yourself have occasion to visit the old city or the Old Town of Dubrovnik after the shelling of 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had you received any information about the extent of the shelling on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The only things that I ever saw were on Belgrade TV, on that -- on those occurrences. And the -- my impression, but it was only my impression from the images that I saw on TV, was that the damage was far more severe than the things that we observed on the 29th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At this time, there is no further direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. If I may, I would like to ask the usher to bring me the rostrum that Ms. Somers has in front of her. Unfortunately, we don't have enough of those plastic things in -- in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Fietelaars. My name is Vlado Petrovic. I represent Mr. Strugar, and I'm going to ask you some questions that arise from your testimony. First of all, I would like to put to you some general questions about your role in the relevant events between the years 1990 and 1992. First of all, can you please tell the Trial Chamber which government took your credentials during that relevant period of time.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the form of the then president, Mr. Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, if you remember, when was it that Mr. Jovic received your credentials?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I can't give you the specific date, but it was within the first two weeks of my arrival in Belgrade. And I arrived in Belgrade on the 3rd of October 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As the Ambassador of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, within your regular duties in Belgrade, who was your regular official contact between October 1990 and May or June 1992? Who was your point of contact for communication with the government in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: In -- in the beginning of that period, it was with the federal government by way of Mr. Loncar, the foreign minister, and in the context of occasional visits to Mr. Markovic who was then the federal president. We also had contacts with different ministries on economic and consular matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me when I say that your contacts with Mr. Loncar were regular up to the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Not regular, sir. They were diminishing from the middle of 1991. The contact was less and less, and contacts about the real preoccupations that the embassy had to express were mainly with the ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you meet Minister Loncar for the last time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I met Minister Loncar for the last time around the same time that the federal presidency was, in fact, reduced to four members. It was Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia, and the representative of Kosovo was still there. By that time, it ceased to be material in our daily dealings, and Mr. Loncar had very little time for us. He was otherwise occupied. And we were often referred to lower civilian contacts within the ministry with whom the message couldn't, after trying to do so, could not be usefully left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the time reference, if you remember. When was this happening?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I can only say, because I did not keep any notes on that type of meeting which did not result in direct reporting. I can only say that it was from the middle of 1991 onwards. The last time I saw Mr. Loncar and talked to him privately, it has just come up in my mind, I'm sorry that it didn't come sooner, that was during the conference of Brioni. And I'm sure that somebody can supply you the direct date of that conference. It has escaped my mind as well. It's all 12 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Prime Minister Anto Markovic at the time, did you have any contacts with him at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But not after the middle of the year, because he spent more time in Zagreb than at Belgrade at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where were the policies of your government and the European Union with regard to the preservation of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, the Netherlands government has for quite some time been trying to stay with the policy that started out as main point. The salvage of the integrity of the Federal Republic. And for the rest, I must say, there's not much that I can add to that because an embassy as such does not deal with that kind of politics. We are there to do incidental work upon instruction on direct issues rather than on general policies. So neither am I an expert, nor do I feel myself qualified to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you informed, were you aware of the policies of your government with regard to the preservation of that state, or was that something that you didn't have to know anything about it, that you didn't know anything about?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: At that time, some personal representatives of our foreign minister were travelling up and down Yugoslavia, and also touched frequently upon Belgrade in order to try and have contact with everybody involved in that process. The embassy on purpose was left outside to do the traditional job of maintaining the relations with the authorities, as we could. Several other people, as I said, were appointed, Hans Van den Broek and travelled up to Belgrade and talked to the people. The embassy never got involved in politics during all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What were your instructions as regarded contacts with the governments of Croatia and Slovenia at that time? We're talking about mid-1992 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, they were parts of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I travelled there as the Netherlands Ambassador to Yugoslavia and talked to the authorities in the context of subjects that were in the main, the competence of those states themselves. But with them, we neither talked about the developments in the Netherlands policy because we had insufficient awareness of it as an embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you escort the representatives of your government who arrived in Belgrade to deal with political issues that had to do with either the breakdown or the survival of Yugoslavia? Did you attend those meetings as the ambassador and the highest representative of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in that country?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have contacts with Stipo Mesic, the president of the presidency of Yugoslavia, in the second half of 1992 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Would you rephrase the question, please. I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As the Ambassador of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, did you have any official contacts with Stipo Mesic, the president of the presidency of the SFRY? And did you have those contacts in the second half of 1991 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I wanted to inquire of the interpreting. The first time the date was raised, it said 1992. And now it says 1991. My concern is that the earlier question about Croatia and Slovenia also was referred to as 1991, but it came out as 1992 in the transcript. Specifically page 53, line 25, seems to have a mid-1992 date in translation. I believe I heard it as 1991. And there may be some confusion. So I would ask that that be clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam. I heard it as --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend is absolutely right on both occasions I inquired about the year 1991. The first question that referred to your contacts with the governments of Croatia and Slovenia was about 1991. And the way I understood your answer, I believe you were referring to 1991. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And the transcript will be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, again in the transcript, we do not have the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It probably got lost in the interruption, Mr. Petrovic. We might have to have it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question was about the contacts that you had with the governments of Croatia and Slovenia in 1991. And you gave your answer about the year 1991. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. And I'm quite willing to rephrase it if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That won't be necessary. Thank you. My second question was as follows: In the second half of 1991, did you have any contacts with the president of the presidency of the SFRY, Mr. Stipo Mesic?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I attended a meeting that took place on the last day of June in Belgrade where the foreign minister of Luxembourg and the foreign minister of the Netherlands were both present to negotiate the federal presidency of Yugoslavia. And the transfer of the European presidency took place in Belgrade between Mr. Poos, foreign minister of Luxembourg, and Hans Van den Broek, foreign minister of the Netherlands. At that meeting, Mr. Mesic was present, but he was not present as -- as such as a Croatian official because he was going to be during that same meeting president of the Federal Republic. So when I met him, it may well be that I met him last there, but I'm not absolutely certain because it escapes my memory. But it may well be that at that meeting that was the last time that I met Mr. Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the Republic of Croatia was recognised by the Kingdom of the Netherlands as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: It must have been in the early part of 1992, but I don't remember the date. In the first half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us why did the government of the Netherlands recognise the Republic of Croatia as late as the first half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I think it has to do with the fact that the Netherlands, until the end of 1991, held the presidency and felt that it was not for the presidency to develop initiative that might either positively or negatively influence other member states. But this is pure speculation. I can't come up with another explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any instructions with regard to your relationship with the governments of Croatia and Slovenia which pronounced their independence unilaterally, regardless of the rest of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Whenever I spoke to people in Zagreb and in Ljubljana, and I spoke to them on specific subjects. And this recognition aspect that you mention was far outside the competency of the embassy. We didn't discuss it, we didn't refer to it, and it never came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind to tell us what were the topics of your discussions in Belgrade, Zagreb, and Ljubljana in that year, if they were not to do with the status of those states, the breakdown of the state, and the new political and state organisation in the area of the western Balkans, as they are called today?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, we were trying to resolve visum arrangements which had ceased to be executed out of Belgrade, and we said that if that is the case, if you want Dutch businessmen to travel to your area or vice versa, we have to do something in order to make that work. Those were specific instructions of the ministry of -- the section of legal affairs in the ministry of Justice who runs that kind of things. And personal contacts, people who had accidents, who died on the road, transport licenses in to pass the autostratus of Slovenia and Croatia in that period because that part of our collaboration had been broken down, and I was instructed to keep it going as well as possible, and to reconstruct it as well as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fietelaars, you were not engaged in political discussions. You only dealt with practical issues that cropped up day in, day out. Would I be correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, that's in essence correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did your government then create its positions about the issues that I've just mentioned if they did not receive any information from you as to what was happening on the ground? Who were the people that informed the government if it wasn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Van den Broek had a special representative to Yugoslavia by the name of Ambassador Wijnaendts who travelled regularly from The Hague and touched upon the capitals of all the member states of the Federal Republic and in Belgrade also had contacts with, for instance, the ministry of Defence very frequently. He reported on that kind of developments to The Hague. And very rarely did I even get a copy of those statements. And (a) it was not necessary for my work, and (b), I could not be drawn into discussions on which I had no authority, no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you send reports on political events in the former Yugoslavia during the relevant period? Did you send those reports to your government in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: My personal evaluations, I certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what were these personal evaluations about?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Mainly about the state of chaos that was slowly taking over, and the difficulties there were for keeping normal administration and normal work going on. And for that, of course, I had contact with ministries, et cetera. But never on the subject that you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fietelaars, I have your report in front of me. The date is 15 October 1991. This report is nothing else but a political report on what was going on in the state. I'm going to read to you several parts of this report. In the first part, you're talking about the declaration that was assigned by Milosevic, Tudjman, and Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be possible if the document is one that has been tendered to at least put it in front of Mr. Fietelaars, or if not, at least give him the benefit of looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document has not been tendered by our learned friends. We are going to tender this into evidence. I'm going to give the witness a copy in Dutch. And I'm also going to have enough copies for everybody. I didn't expect that this witness is going to say before this Trial Chamber that he didn't know anything about the political events in Yugoslavia. After the first break, I'm going to make copies and tender it into evidence. And now, I would like to give the ambassador the Dutch copy of his report for his perusal. Can you please give the copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what the subject of this report is. And this is to be seen on the first page of this report.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The subject is, "Political developments in Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the first paragraph on page 1. Here, you inform your government about the declaration that was signed in Igalo by Milosevic, Tudjman, and Kadijevic after the meeting that was held there.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was there at that meeting. And I -- there has been a report on that meeting. I think that Britain, Lord Carrington, was presiding the delegation at the time. And I remind the people that I report to about part of the text of the declaration of Igalo which was free knowledge. So it's more of a journalistic remark than a reporting remark. But this is -- this document, I have written. And it was true, all parties stated that they recognised the -- the solutions proposed in the declaration of Igalo as the last chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, look at paragraph 5 in which you're talking about your evaluations as for the hopes for a peaceful solution to the civil war that was still going on. This is your evaluation and the way you described the things that were going on.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your evaluation of what was happening at the time, is it the same as described here? That is, that it was a civil war.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: That was my personal opinion, yes, sir. But this was not based upon meetings with high officials of either the Federal Republic or the states of Yugoslavia. This was a concerned person living in Belgrade watching the TV, talking to people, and coming to conclusions that I write down here on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible, Mr. Fietelaars, that the ambassador of the Kingdom of the Netherlands receives information mostly from the media? I assume that you would have had numerous contacts with all the major players in those events at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Could you define "major players," sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Members of the government, the federal government, the republican governments, various governmental ministers, influential politicians, heads of political parties. This is the way I perceive the job of an ambassador. My perception may be wrong as to what the duties and contacts of the ambassador of such a powerful and influential state as the Kingdom of the Netherlands may be, especially in the light of the fact that your state was presiding over the European Union at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Your perception is correct insofar as that I talked to representatives of political parties, just like the journalists did. I did not give them any insight, and neither could I, in the thinkings of my minister on future recognition or anything. I listened, I observed, I evaluated, and I wrote. And that is the function of an ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You have a lot of experience; you had a lot of experience already when you found yourself in the turmoil of the civil war in the former Yugoslavia. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your evaluation that this was a civil war was based on your rich experience and the facts that you saw all around you. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph -- the third or the fourth paragraph talking about the process of political disintegration in Macedonia. Can you see that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment. The fourth paragraph -- yes, I've found it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at that paragraph and tell us whether the report of yours contains positions on the political processes which were taking place in Bosnia and Macedonia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I don't really know what the question is. That I reported what I heard? We heard from people within the cabinet of Mr. Izetbegovic information about how the meetings actually went. I reported on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your role, judging by this report, was not what you told us, that it was you were well informed about all the political processes that were taking place in the former Yugoslavia at the time. Would I be correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I was informed or I informed myself? I don't know. I was informed. It was not that an avalanche of unsolicited information reached the embassy. I talked to people, I travelled, and I observed what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The reports that you sent to The Hague, were your conclusions drawn from the truthful or truthful to the biggest possible extent facts that you heard about, because you were sending reports to your government?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes. It would be pretty useless if only dry facts were presented, while I had an embassy in Belgrade that lived there and worked there and formed opinion on the basis of information and -- and experience received. That is the function of an embassy. So not only documents with facts were referred, but also my interpretation of them and my evaluation of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please finish your answer. I've interrupted you, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to say that if you read the second part of the paragraph that you refer to, that I tried to make a summary of a document I received. And the second document also I give a summary that is received, and then I say, "We will receive English translations from the document, and that they will be faxed to the embassy as soon as they are ready. As soon as they are ready, the embassy will make use of them."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, look at one paragraph but last, towards the end of this document, where you talk about Milosevic and the Greater Serbia. Can you please explain the difference between the aspirations that Milosevic had according to you and the aspirations of the Yugoslav People's Army. What is this all about? Are these goals convergent? I am just trying to talk about your report written on the 15 of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: May I read it, please, sir. I think, sir, that this has to do with initiatives about finding a solution to the rising problems between member states of the republic and that the changes in border that could or would be used to find such solution were not considered by all member states as identical. That everybody had his own solution, and that it was noticeable, and maybe for somebody living in Belgrade it was more noticeable what the Serbian attitude was because we watched Serb television in Belgrade. That solution by the change of borders was not at that time seeming to become -- to become a solution of the problem. And that increasing hard positions hanging on to initially made points of view were clear in all the circumstances, in the press, in talks, in discussions, and on television. And on the basis of this document, the last thing says also for Bosnia-Herzegovina, that parliament does not believe in --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. Can you please focus on my question. My question was, what is the difference between the ambitions of the JNA to preserve their role and what you describe here as Milosevic's aspiration towards the Greater Serbia? Is there a difference? If there is, what is the difference between these two sets of ambitions or these two programmes? Milosevic's on the one hand, and those of the JNA on the other, both of which you mention in your report.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't have a clue about in how far they are identical or converging or diverging. I make reports on what I see and what I evaluate. And that has never been part of this kind of evaluation, to compare points of view taken by the JNA and points of view taken by the Serbian presidency in Belgrade. The JNA I dealt with on the basis of instructions received on incidental things that happened, never on policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA, or rather, the leadership of the JNA that you contacted with as opposed to Milosevic want to perform its constitutional role and preserve the country as provided for by the constitution of that same country? Is that the conclusion that can be drawn from what you say in the penultimate paragraph of your report of the 15th of October?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No. It doesn't make any reference to the JNA, and I don't think it has anything to do with the JNA. But every time that Admiral Brovet or General Kadijevic has said to me that that was the function that you describe was the function of the JNA and that they were executing their function to the best of their ability and to the honour of their profession, every time they said it, every time I reported that to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This report, does it represent the sum total of what you were told, or is it your synthetic analysis and work, your conclusions, your understanding of the political processes and the role of the actors in those processes? Because this is what you say here. You say apart from that the aspirations toward a Greater Serbia by Milosevic would include Serbia and Montenegro alone would preserve its -- the role it has occupied until the present time, or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, that's my conclusion. I think that the development and the cost of the conflict was such that the JNA would also feel the consequences of the tremendous cost of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So therefore you agree that there is a difference in the goals and aims of the JNA on the one hand, and Milosevic on the other?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I don't refer to that. The fact that I say that it will have its consequences for the viability for the JNA is a conclusion that I have drawn, and the fact that Mr. Milosevic pushed with greater insistence his original plan for the solution of the conflict is another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a different subject. But they are two different goals altogether, at least judging by what you have written here.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: But I don't see where I talk about the goals of the JNA. The goals of the JNA, I assume, are the execution of their functions. In the execution of its functions, there are dangers when your money supply runs out drastically. That's the only thing I say here. But it doesn't necessarily change the objects of the JNA. I assume that the objects of the JNA are defined by the Supreme Command in Belgrade, at that time being Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, whether in your opinion the time we're discussing, that period, whether in your opinion the state with which you communicated and to which you were accredited had all the formal attributes of a legitimate, a legitimate state authority for the territory we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The embassy did not address that question, nor should it address that question. That's not for the embassy. I as an ambassador have observed that contacts at the highest level of the Federal Republic became more difficult in the course of the time that I was accredited to Belgrade. That's the only thing political, if you want to call it political, that I have to say. The communication possibilities with the top of the federal government, and including the JNA, became more difficult as time went on. And that, in fact, is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If as an ambassador you didn't have the duty to follow political processes, did you as an experienced individual have your own conclusions as to whether you were accredited to a legitimate, existing, ordered state or not? If you didn't deal with that pursuant to the descriptions of the job you held, which I doubt; but if you say so, I believe you.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The last -- the last two-thirds of the last linea of this report are exclusively for my responsibility. They are my conclusions on the basis of what I heard, saw, was informed, by all kind of means, and by what I observed myself. That, I think, is the function of an ambassador. It's not the function of an ambassador to go into politics for himself. It is to execute the instructions of his government and to gather information, interpret that information, and get both the information and his interpretation to his home government. And if the embassy is not that, then I failed in my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If we may conclude, your government didn't give you any political instructions, but gave you only instructions which had to do with solving problems such as visa problems, trade, the problems of businessmen, et cetera. So the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the second half of 1991 had no political instructions coming out from its ministry in The Hague to you. Would I be right in concluding it that way? Whereas this report represents your initiative on your part informing them on subjects that surpass your competence and authorisation. Would that be it, then?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, sir, that would be the wrong conclusion. When I talked about no political instruction, no political contacts, no political activities, I was referring to your question about what I did in Zagreb and in Ljubljana and in the capitals of the member state when I talked to people there. In Belgrade, I received instructions, and of course they were political to go and see Mr. Brovet and tell him about the worries and preoccupations of the Netherlands, or of the European Union as the case might be, and try and solicit an answer to these preoccupations from the authorities that I transmitted these preoccupations to. In the course of the discussions and the conversations that developed in those meetings, I made my judgement about how the instruction -- the execution of the instructions was received by the receiving authorities, and I added my comments on the basis of what I listened to during those conversations. That was the function of the embassy, and that's what I did. So that part of it was political, but it had nothing to do with whether or not my government was considering to recognise or derecognise any authority in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fietelaars, did your government in the autumn of 1991 persevere along the political position that the SFRY should be preserved as a political community of south Slav peoples, yes or no, or did you never receive instructions to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I attended the conference of Brioni in the company of my minister, and there it a decision was made that for the next three months nothing was going to be changed in the status quo of the political situation in Yugoslavia. My government, as far as I could observe, acted along those lines, and when further developments, both nationally in Yugoslavia and internationally, warranted it, they adjusted to what was then already a concrete actuality. But saying that we went on dealing with the federal government and such, I told you communication was more difficult and more difficult. And very often one had to choose between the departments that were competent for certain issues or the Supreme Command of the JNA, at the same time being the presidency of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was a difficult role most of the times. And it probably played a role in recognising the constituting parts as new entities in the long run. But this embassy I ran up to the middle of 1992 was not involved in that process. For that, the Netherlands government had an gentleman called Ambassador Wijnaendts, and he ran that part of the show.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that in November 1991, the position of the government of the Kingdom of the Netherlands was that the SFRY should be preserved?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I don't think you can put that position as such. The Netherlands acted upon their observance that the SFRY functioned at that moment to a certain extent and could still be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was the position the same of the government of Holland in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what the position was of your government in January 1992, for example?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, sir. At that time, there was no discussion going on about that subject in the internal Netherlands administration as far as it could be observed by this embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document, the one that I showed to Mr. Fietelaars, I should like to tender into evidence immediately after the break. It is a document that was otherwise disclosed by the Prosecution, and my learned colleague I'm sure is aware of its contents. But since I wasn't able to foresee the course that the cross-examination would take, I haven't prepared it as yet. And I hope you will understand my position in that regard and my explanation given. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fietelaars, may I now move on to some other aspects of the topic we're discussing. Can you tell this Honourable Trial Chamber who had Supreme Command over the armed forces of the SFRY during the period we're discussing, that is to say, the second half of 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: According to the people that we talked within the JNA, they received orders from the Supreme Command in the person of President Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who pursuant to the SFRY constitution actually embodies and represents the Supreme Command of the armed forces? If not, we can move on straight away.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm aware of it, that it is the president of the federal presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The president of the federal presidency, is he, then, therefore the legitimate person in taking decisions with regard to the deployment of the armed forces of the SFRY for the material time that we're discussing?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: That is not a matter that can be judged neither by me or in the attitudes of the embassy. I know that preoccupations existed, not only in the Netherlands, but in many other states as well, for the diminishing size of the federal presidency and the absence of what, in fact, was in the end at least half of the presidency, so that majorities could not be established any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the government of the Kingdom of the Netherlands assume the position that the Yugoslav People's Army was a legitimate armed force of the SFRY in the month of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I think that the embassy, at least, and I can only speak for the embassy, I can't speak for the government of the Netherlands, that the embassy assumed that the JNA was our right opposite number because there was no other authority that fulfilled that specific function in the structures that remained upright in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did your embassy in December 1991 consider the Yugoslav People's Army to be the legitimate armed force of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The word "legitimate" doesn't come into it. It was the actual force in Belgrade fulfilling that function. And the embassy has no competence in judging the legitimacy of instruments of Yugoslav government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you, as the ambassador in the country, know how that country functioned, what its organs and institutions were, what their competencies and authorisation was?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I can only say that I observed what actually took place. I talked to people who were closer to those instruments and institutions that you refer to than I was. And on the basis of information received, I probably -- I certainly, strike appropriate people [sic] -- I certainly informed the Netherlands government that the JNA was the only military authority that we could contact in order to discuss instructions with the military dimension emanating from the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that with the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs in December of 1991, and that was the sole and exclusive body that you had official cooperation with as a representative of the Dutch government?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The only thing that I know is that by that time, there was nobody in the building that houses the foreign ministry of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with whom I could deal. There were a number of functionaries who kept the building open. But appointments on any subject were impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you didn't communicate with anybody in the government, except for the representatives of the JNA at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: A grossa mora [phoen], that is correct. We dropped specific letters in the hands of the people who still were in the building of foreign affairs with a request to send them on to the competent authorities. And I assume that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who did you address them to, those letters? Who were the addressees, the addresses, the president of the Yugoslav state Presidency, the prime minister, who?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: We did not communicate with the prime minister. We did communicate to the temporary minister of foreign affairs who acted when Mr. Loncar was not there any more. I do not remember his name at present, but I am sure that you can look it up, who took over for Mr. Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the first time you communicated with Loncar's deputy in 1992, the beginning of 1992, that that was the first time you had any contacts with him? And there are written traces of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I don't know what "traces" mean, but if that is so, then that is so. But I had contact with the gentleman already long before because he was a foreign minister, the number two of Mr. Loncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his name was, the gentleman you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I'm trying to dig it out, but I can't find it. I will let you know as soon as it comes up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the other organs and institutions were of the state to which you were accredited, the federal government, who led the federal government, what its function was, et cetera, et cetera, the ministries, the federal ministries, and so on? Do you know anything about that, the various departments?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We had an organogram of the whole structures of the federal government and we used it. However, there's not much use in questioning me about it, because it's 12 years ago, and I wouldn't know any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we take the break perhaps now, because I shall be moving on to a different area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. That's probably a convenient time, Mr. Petrovic. We'll have another break now, Mr. Fietelaars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fietelaars, I should now like to ask you to tell us what you, during the material time, knew about the command structure of the Yugoslav People's Army. How was it organised? Who headed it, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Sir, I can't help you very much there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could the microphones be turned on for the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The structure of the embassy was such that we had a military attache and a number of people who worked for him who kept us up to date insofar as it was possible on the basis of the information received from the military authorities about who was where and who did what. Their work as far as the organogram was concerned was mainly interesting for my military attache for reporting to his authorities. And I had little or no interest in that structure, except as far as it was necessary to identify the people that I needed to speak with. And that I did with the help of my military attache. And so if you want me to lecture on the structures in the JNA, you -- I'll have to respectfully decline.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fietelaars, I, of course, do not expect you to do that. But I would like you to answer some questions which in view of the position you yourself held were quite logical, and I expect you know the answer to them and will provide us with one. Your military attache, what did he tell you with respect to who was at the head of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: For that, I didn't need any information. We got a briefing upon arrival from a colonel of the JNA about the top of the ministry of Defence, including the military officers who were on active service but posted in Belgrade. And whom to address about what, we got a paper on that, and I took that with me to the embassy and used it to decide which gentlemen to telephone whenever I had to drop a message or whether -- and my officers in the embassy used the same paper to decide which gentlemen they had to approach with the messages that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your answer is rather lengthy. So may I ask you to be more specific in response to my questions, please. And along those lines, how in the document that was presented to you obviously, how -- what were the addresses? Who did you have to refer to for what within the frameworks of the JNA structure? What were you told on this document, the one you had before you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: The address of the ministry of Defence. I don't even know the street any more. But this is one of the long main streets of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I'm not, of course, asking you about the address literally. I'm not talking about that. I'm talking figuratively who you would contact, of course, and not the address in the literal term of the street.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Me being the ambassador, the logical contacts were the commander of the JNA, which at the start of my presence in Belgrade was General Kadijevic, or his number two who was Admiral Brovet. Officers of my embassy usually dealt with the liaison officer of the ministry, which for most of the time that I was there was a colonel named Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And which questions were questions addressed to General Kadijevic that merited his being involved?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Whenever I received instructions that I should contact the JNA at the highest possible level, I approached General Kadijevic. There were a number of preoccupations. There were a number of occasions to rise questions, and a number of occasions where to give information. I did that whenever I got in instruction to touch the highest possible level of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you help us out, please. What type of problems did you bring before General Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: All problems that had to do with preoccupations concerning the well-being of the people in certain regions, places where military activities or irregular activities took place. And everything where the information reached us that the JNA were involved in certain things where we would want to verify what actually was the reality, which -- what actually was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who else was there on your list of individuals whom you could redress for information about certain matters, in addition to General Kadijevic, of course, and Colonel Stojic, if I remember correctly. Who else?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: As I said, Colonel Stojic. And for the rest, in the course of the time, varying officers whose position started at the JNA headquarters or stopped at the JNA headquarters, I don't recollect the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In view of what you just told us and what you took to General Kadijevic, could you tell us the problems you took to the others whose names you can't remember today?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I personally only talked to Kadijevic and Brovet. The rest of the embassy talked to the other officers, and they took every problem, cooperation, presence at each other's exercises, all kind of military stuff. And in general, detailed information that I did not occupy myself with, but that I entrusted to one of my officers. That's why I have staff in an embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to what you have just told us, did you know anything else about the organisation of the Yugoslav People's Army and the structure of its command, or does this pretty much sum up all that you knew about the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: At the time, I think I recollected a lot more of the top of the organogram of the JNA. But in the 12 years ago in between, all of that has disappeared because it was never very relevant to me, and certainly after leaving Yugoslavia it was not relevant to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know what the competencies of the 5th military district were?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I don't even know what the location of the 5th military district was, so the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what about the military naval district? Did you know what was the area of its authority?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Naval district, I assume you refer to the 9th district -- in that case, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the term, "military naval district"? Did you ever hear this area referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who General Raseta is?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that he was rather visible on Yugoslav television in the course of the military activities in Croatia, around Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear or are you familiar with the 1st Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of or are you aware of the units which were stationed in the area of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I was aware of the presence of the JNA in the area of Vukovar, but not which units were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what about the 2nd Operational Group? Did you ever hear of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I may have, but I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what about the area of responsibility of the 2nd Operational Group? Did you ever hear what that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I may well have, but I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you maybe know who the commander of the 1st Operational Group was?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with any military unit in the territory of the SFRY in the months of October, November, and December 1991?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How come that in your report you mentioned the 9th naval sector or district?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: We were briefed before our departure from Belgrade to Tivat by Colonel Stojic, and I think that he referred to the 9th naval district. And if my report says he referred to the 9th naval district, or I refer to the 9th naval district, that is the source, and that was the expression that was used. By the way, translation was being used because Colonel Stojic addressed us in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with any other military unit during the relevant period of time in addition to this 9th naval district?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: We had a military office in the embassy with a military attache, a deputy military attache, an archivist and a researcher. Those people were very much aware of the answers to the questions that you pose. I did not occupy myself with those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Kindly tell us, how come that after 14 years you can recall just one military unit, and this being the 9th naval district? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: That is because I recently reread my reports from that time on the basis of this meeting here. And in that report, it's explicitly mentioned that we were going to meet the commanding officers of the 9th naval district. So that is how that name came back to my mind. And the others haven't come up yet because I have had no reason to re-research the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the reports that you reviewed, are there any other units mentioned, except for the 9th naval district?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Sir, my recent research limited itself to the happenings around Dubrovnik in the period of October, November, December of that year. And I don't think that in the documents that I looked at in that context any other area or any other units were mentioned. It would have been irrelevant information because in the foreign ministry in The Hague, nobody would have to know what to do with such detailed information. As I said, for that, we had military attaches, also in Yugoslavia and in our capitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The only military unit that you mention in reference to the events around Dubrovnik is this one, the 9th naval district. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I thought the 9th naval district referred to a place, rather than to a unit. An area. Which would make the word "district" appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the 9th naval sector? Is that the only unit that is mentioned in your reports with regard to the events around Dubrovnik, or did you mention any other units as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I did not -- I just referred to JNA troops and Croatian people in and around Dubrovnik. I never mentioned any units. The word I used was put in my mind by Colonel Stojic. That's the only reason why it was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Colonel Stojic tell you that the area of responsibility around Dubrovnik was the area of responsibility of the 9th naval district?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I assume he did because I think -- I -- yes, I did [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you that the commander of the 9th naval district would receive you in audience?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: He said we were going to be received by two high-ranking officers in the region. And that was the reference that he used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: During your visit, did you realise that it was Jokic who was the commander of the 9th naval district because he was your host and he was involved in all the aspects of your visit?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I didn't assume anything. I knew that high-ranking officers were going to meet us upon arrival. There was a high-ranking officer upon our arrival, so I assumed he was Mr. Stojic -- Mr. Jokic. And it went on from there. I didn't draw any conclusions out of the fact of the way in which we were received about the command structure of the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was your impression at the end of that day with regard to the command and who was the leader who received you, who gave you all the instructions, who told you to go back, and who organised a meal for you? Did you draw any conclusions based on all that as to who was in charge there?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Sir, at the afternoon meeting after our return from Dubrovnik, we met two high-ranking officers. I assumed, and that may have been just an assumption in the way you pose your questions by now, that they were Admiral Jokic and General Strugar. I had not met the gentlemen in person before. I had seen Mr. Jokic in the ministry, and he was pointed out to me. And I had seen him on television. I had never seen Mr. Strugar before, nor have I ever seen him since. But when I was there, I assumed that I was introducing myself to General Strugar and Admiral Jokic. And if that was a wrong impression, the impression was created by the introduction and by the fact that nobody contradicted that or introduced themselves by a different name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say a high-ranking officer, what does that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: You should ask Colonel Stojic. He used the term, not I.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the ranks on these two people that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before this event, where did you used to see Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: On Belgrade TV. He had been reasonably visible in the weeks before. And at one meeting that we had in the ministry, either with Admiral Brovet or with General Kadijevic, where somebody pointed out to me a general with the name of Jokic. And he looked quite similar to the gentleman I met in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe this gentleman, this Admiral Jokic, very briefly. Could you provide us with a very short description of this person.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Sir, it's 14 years ago. It's not -- I haven't been trained to describe faces or anything. No, I can't. It was a military officer who was obviously the centre of the presence at the Yugoslav side. I introduced myself to him. He shook my hands and smiled. It limited itself to that, except for the general conversation in the second meeting. And I cannot describe him. No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, at the meetings where you saw Kadijevic, Brovet, and Jokic, what topics were discussed at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: At that specific meeting, I don't remember. I just remember that during one of the meetings he was pointed out to me, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was one of the topics also operations around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I can't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: There's no translation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would it be logical for one of the topics to be Dubrovnik, given the fact that he was in command in the territory of the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to speculate on the logicality or the probability of such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was your impression about the role of Admiral Jokic in view of the first meeting that you had with Kadijevic, Brovet, and Jokic? What was your impression about his role in this entire military issue?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I wasn't introduced to him. He was pointed out to me during one meeting. That was an admiral called Jokic. And was that the full extent of my information. So I don't really know what he was doing there. There were a number of officers sitting around and behind the spokesman that were talking to me, and in this case I, Admiral Brovet or General Kadijevic. And they were there. I don't know why they were there. For decoration or supplying additional information or whatever. That's the way these things are done, and I don't draw any conclusions from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How come that you spotted Jokic immediately? There are probably a lot of meetings, a lot of people. It was a long time ago. How come you remember Jokic? How come you spotted him right away?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Because he was pointed out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Kindly tell us, what was the main source or what it is that you refer to today when you tried to reconstruct the events that took place in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Could you rephrase the question, please. I don't understand what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'll try. I'll do my best. I'm sorry that you didn't understand me the first time. What is it that assists you today when you try to recall the events that you're talking about here today?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I'm assisted by a number of papers that I kept because of the modus operandi that I used when I was ambassador of Yugoslavia. Whenever the day ended I put on paper the things that I wanted to put on paper, facts, interpretations, or what have you. They got refined in the course of the evening. And in the early morning, they were put into coded messages and sent to The Hague. And the first drafts of my considerations on the day before, I kept in a separate folder, and I stacked one on the other. And I have been able to consult these things when they asked me, "Do you recollect what went on in that period?" I said, "I will check my sources and come back to you." And that is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether your testimony would be practically impossible without these notes? Could you remember the names, the places, the events, or is your recollection mostly based on your notes and the notes that you have recently referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: But the large lines of my memory, of course, stayed in my mind. But all the details have been the result of recent research in things that I wrote by hand myself at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the general impressions about the events, whatever concerns, and people, dates, places, meetings, all of that is something that you were able to remember while you were consulting your notes?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The details and the specifics, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, would it be correct that your notes and your reports were done diligently, conscientiously, correctly, that they contained the most important things, that you left no stone unturned, that you didn't omit anything?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I don't know how you work, but that's not how I work. I try to retain the most important things that I want to retain. And I write them down, and I do not try to touch upon everything that happened that day. I take the larger lines and the things that remain in my mind as important. They are put on paper diligently and upon my honour as a hard-working man who loves his country and does a job for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your notes and the information that you send to your ministry contain everything that you deemed important about whom you had met and what had been discussed at each and every of these meetings. Would I be correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: No, you would not be correct, sir, because that was what was needed to be transmitted at the time. Very often other subjects came up, and I used that information that hadn't been used before to insert it in reports of the following weeks or months, or in consolidated reports based upon my evaluation of what I saw going on in the weeks that were past. So it was not the end of the use of my information by the time a message was transmitted to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If, for example, you had had a meeting with a high-ranking officer of the JNA, and if there was a need to report on that meeting, would your information contain the name of the person that you talked to, when and what the subjects of your conversation were?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Very often information was depersonalised, that we referred to authorities in that or that ministry, or spokesmen of this or that. There was no need to confuse the situation in The Hague by using names. We used functions mainly in reporting in order to keep the information lines clear. Lots of people share names, and you cause confusion if you start to describe the events by name rather than by function.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. Therefore, in your reports, you always mentioned only the most important names in order to avoid confusion with your superiors in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Information that I received from the top of the JNA, being Mr. Kadijevic and Mr. Brovet, was always referred to by name because these names were known in The Hague, and it indicated a phenomenon as much as a person and a function. So on that basis, we used names. Below that level, I never used names because, as I said, it confused people, and it may well be that my officers in reporting directly to the authorities to which they were supposed to report went further in detail because details are shared, for instance, between military people who have served for a long time and know each other across borders. But as far as political information was, I had to have it to depersonalise it as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: However, you did mention some most important military commanders. Maybe one or two in addition to Brovet and Kadijevic. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mentioned, for instance, the name Stojic. I mentioned the name Strugar. I mentioned the name Jokic in a report where I spent part of the day with these gentlemen and where, for variety's sake and for readability sake, the one time you say the Admiral, and the next time you say Admiral Jokic, and the next time when you are in your conclusions and you try to keep it short and concise, you only use the name without reference to Mr. or rank. Everybody does it in his own way. That's the way in which I did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I wanted to ask you, sir. Did you ever in any of your reports mention the name of General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: JOHANNES FIETELAARS
utterances.text: I think I did. But they are mainly in the context of relating things that were told to me within the ministry of Defence, because otherwise -- especially from the sources outside the ministry of Defence, I never referred to officials by name because I might myself become the subject of confusion rather than The Hague.
